help.title: Guide
help.subtitle: Everything the application can do, point by point: where to find each feature and how to use it.

start.title: First steps
start.where: applies the first time the application is opened.
start.figure: The toolbar at the top of the library: this is where the music comes in the first time.
steps: The library starts empty: the first step is telling the application where the music is.
Use "Add folder" to bring in a whole folder and its subfolders in one go.
When the import ends, a summary reports how many tracks came in, how many were already there and which ones could not be read.
The Tracks, Artists, Albums and Genres tabs show the same library grouped in four ways.
Double-click a track to listen to it: the list on screen becomes the playback queue.
Everything else — columns, appearance, player behaviour — is set from the settings, behind the gear in the title bar.
start.tip: If a library was already exported from another installation, import it from Settings → Library instead of starting from the folders again.

import.title: Adding tracks and folders
import.where: top bar of the Library, or by dropping onto the window.
import.figure: The commands that add tracks and folders.
steps: Press "Add tracks" to choose one or more audio files, or "Add folder" to import all the music in a folder and its subfolders.
You can also drop files or folders onto the window: the library lights up to say it is ready for them.
Formats read: MP3, FLAC, M4A, OGG and WAV.
The same file never enters twice: one already in the library is counted among the skipped ones.
A summary then says what was added, what was already there and what could not be imported; a clean import closes itself.
The files stay where they are: importing only reads them, it does not copy, move or rename them. The library keeps the list of where they sit.
import.tip: The files stay where they are: move a folder after importing it and its tracks read as missing until they are imported again from the new place.

organize.title: Searching, filtering and sorting
organize.where: top bar, column headers and library menu.
organize.figure: The search field and the library menu, with the filters and the tools.
steps: Type in the search field to filter by title, artist, album, genre or path.
Click a column header to sort; a second click on the same column turns the order around.
In the preview views, which have no headers, use the sort control beside the view switch.
Tracks without that field always sink to the bottom, in both directions.
"Missing data", in the library menu, leaves on screen only the tracks without a cover, an artist, an album, a year or a genre.
The count beside the tabs says how many items the open tab holds.
organize.tip: Sorting, searching and filtering never touch the files: they only change the way the list is shown.

views.title: Views, tabs and connections
views.where: the two icons on the right of the bar, and the tabs under it.
views.figure: The switch between list and cards, at the end of the toolbar.
steps: The list icon shows the columns, the grid icon shows the covers; the choice is remembered.
The Tracks, Artists, Albums and Genres tabs gather the same library in four ways.
A click on an artist, an album or a genre opens the window of the tracks connected to it.
From there you can go further down: from an album to its artist, from an artist to their albums, from a genre to its artists.
The button at the top left of that window goes back, and names where it lands.
Which columns the list shows, and in which order, is set from "Columns" in the library menu.
views.tip: The view, the size of the cards and the layout of the columns are remembered separately for each tab.

metadata.title: Editing the metadata
metadata.where: the three dots menu on the row or on the card, or a right click on the row.
metadata.figure: The three-dot menu on the row of the track.
steps: Open the three dots menu, or right click the row, and choose Edit.
Change title, artist, album, year and genre; the genre can be picked among the ones already in the library or typed.
With "Choose image…" you replace the cover (PNG or JPEG, up to 5 MB).
Press "Save": the changes are written into the tags of the file, not only into the library.
Leaving a field empty removes that value from the file.
Selecting several tracks with Ctrl or Shift brings up "Edit selected": it writes the same value on all of them.
metadata.tip: Before editing many tracks at once, try a single one: the change is written into the files and cannot be undone.

files.title: Working on the files
files.where: library menu and the three dots menu on the row.
steps: Opening a library reads the files again: tags edited by another program arrive on their own, and files that left their place are reported with a banner and an icon on the row.
"Check files", in the library menu, runs the check on request and says how many are missing.
"Find duplicates" lists the tracks held in more than one file, matched by title with its artist or by file name.
From there you can remove the copy too many: it leaves the library, the file stays on disk.
"Delete", in the row menu, takes the track out of the list without deleting anything from the disk.
A track whose file is gone can be neither edited nor played, but stays listed until you remove it.
files.tip: A file reported missing that still exists has almost always been moved: import it again from its new place and drop the old entry.

player.title: Listening to the music
player.where: double click a row or a card; the player appears at the bottom.
player.figure: The player along the bottom, with the controls and the progress bar.
steps: Double click the track to listen to: the list you are looking at becomes the queue.
The player at the bottom carries cover, title, artist, progress, volume and mute.
Shuffle and repeat one change the way the queue moves on.
The arrow at the top right of the player opens the full view, the X closes the playback.
In the full view artist, album and genre are links: they open the connected tracks, and from there another one can be started.
The settings can leave the player on screen, minimized, even after the track is closed.
player.tip: Stop rewinds without emptying the queue: the track starts again from the beginning.

dock.title: Floating player
dock.where: appears when the app goes to the system tray while something is playing.
dock.figure: The floating player and its controls.
steps: The low dash button, in the title bar, sends the app to the system tray: the playback carries on.
With a track playing, the floating player appears: a small window with cover, title and controls.
It is moved by dragging it from any free spot.
Its menu turns it between horizontal and vertical, and decides whether it stays above other windows.
The expand button brings the application back on screen and closes the floating player.
Closing it asks whether to quit the application or leave it in the system tray: the answer can be remembered.
dock.tip: The place the floating player was left in is remembered: it comes back where it was.

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts and gestures
shortcuts.where: the track list, the player and the detail windows.
steps: Double-click a row or a card: playback starts.
Right-click a row: the same menu as the three dots opens.
Ctrl + click adds a track to the selection, Shift + click takes the whole range.
Esc closes the open window and, from the full player view, returns to the library.
Dropping files or folders on the window imports them without going through the buttons.
Dragging the edge between two headings changes the width of a column; the command next to the gear fits them to their content.
shortcuts.tip: The search field works on title, artist, album, genre and path at once: one word is usually enough to narrow the list.

libraries.title: More than one library
libraries.where: the two arrows icon beside the name, and Settings → Library.
libraries.figure: The two-arrow icon next to the name of the library.
steps: Each library has its own list of tracks: one for everyday music, one for work, and so on.
The two arrows icon beside the name opens the quick switch between libraries.
In Settings → Library a new library is created from the field at the top of the section.
Pick a library from the list to arm the commands above it: export, rename and set as main.
The main library is the one that opens at startup; "Open" and "Delete" stay on the row of each.
Deleting a library removes only its list: the audio files are left untouched.
libraries.tip: The primary library is the one that opens at launch: point it at the one used most.

transfer.title: Importing and exporting
transfer.figure: The import and export section of the settings.
steps: "Export library" saves a file with the list of tracks and their data, covers included.
Importing a library asks how to merge it: replace the open one, add only the new tracks, or update the ones already there as well.
A summary then says how many tracks entered, how many were updated, how many skipped and which files could not be found.
"Export list" saves instead a text or CSV file with the fields you choose: it is meant to be read elsewhere.
An exported list holds no audio: it always refers to where the files are on disk.
transfer.tip: To carry the library to another computer, export the file and import it there: the paths still have to lead to the same audio files.

appearance.title: Appearance
steps: Text size: four steps, from very small to large, scaling the whole interface.
Theme: light, dark, or the one of the system.
Accent colour: the colour of the controls, of the selection and of the gradient background.
Background and glass: turns on the gradient built from the accent, picks its shape and its origin, and makes the surfaces translucent. It can be carried onto the detail windows too.
Background colour from the cover: the player takes its colour from the cover of the track; transparency, intensity, blur, shape and origin are all adjustable.
Every choice applies at once and is remembered for the next time.
appearance.tip: If the interface feels heavy on a slow machine, turn the glass effect and the ambient background off.

settings.title: Startup, window and general
settings.where: Settings → General, and the title bar.
settings.figure: The gear in the title bar, which opens the settings.
steps: Language: Italian, English, French, Spanish and German, applied immediately.
Startup and window: start the app with the system, start minimized in the system tray, and stay there on close instead of quitting.
From the tray a click reopens the window, a right click offers to stop the playback or to quit.
Player: leave the player open after the track is closed, and set the floating player — when it appears, whether it stays on top, its layout and what closing it does.

Default audio player: on Windows it opens the system settings to associate audio files with this app; on Linux the association belongs to the desktop environment, and the section shows the command to run.
The "i" button in the title bar opens the about window: version, website, project on GitHub, release notes and published releases.
settings.tip: Start with the system and start minimised work together: with both on, the app is already waiting in the system tray.

storage.title: Your files and the app’s data
storage.where: everywhere; the cover cache is in Settings → Library.
steps: Importing reads your files where they are: it does not copy them, move them or rename them. The library keeps only the list of where they sit.
Metadata changes are written into the file itself, in place: the write goes onto a temporary copy that replaces the original only once it is complete, so an interruption cannot ruin the file.
Taking a track out of the list, or deleting a library, deletes nothing from the disk.
The app keeps its own data — settings and libraries — in a folder of your user profile; covers taken from your files are kept in a cache of their own, so they need not be read again at every start.

The cache keeps itself under a limit: past it, the covers asked for longest ago are dropped. Settings → Library shows what it takes up and empties it whenever you like; it rebuilds itself, and your files are left alone.
Nothing leaves your computer: no internet connection, no telemetry, no data sent anywhere.
storage.tip: Emptying the cover cache loses nothing: the covers are read from the files again when they are next needed.
